title: A step forward in Jamia, a long road ahead
where: The Editorial Page, page 12 (Editorial); report on page 4
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to education; Democratic participation · GS1 › Youth and society · GS4 › Trust, dialogue and leadership
summary: After an 18-day protest, Jamia Millia Islamia agreed to restore student union elections, dissolved since 2006, within a fixed timeline.
ideas: A guideline turned into a ban: the Lyngdoh Committee (2005) wanted to curb money, muscle power and outside political influence in campus polls; universities used it to scrap elections altogether.
GS2 · Education governance
Reforms meant to clean up student politics have often been used to suspend it.
Campus democracy is a school of citizenship: elections open campus decisions to students and give their grievances a channel; their absence infantilises young adults.
GS2 · Democracy / GS1 · Youth
Student union elections train young adults in representative democracy and grievance redress.
Trust, not restriction: disciplinary action and curbs on essential services deepened the breakdown of trust; resolution came only through talks and a fixed timeline.
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Dialogue
Fixed timelines and dialogue resolve campus disputes better than punitive discipline.
A wider pattern: Karnataka has approved student polls, Madhya Pradesh saw judicial intervention, Maharashtra set up a committee and Odisha is holding talks.
GS2 · Federal practice in education
Several states are reviving student elections, showing a shift towards participatory campuses.
Youth demands for accountability: the protest echoed the movement at Aligarh Muslim University and the wider Gen Z protests seeking a say in decisions.
GS1 · Youth / Social change
Campus movements reflect a wider youth demand for voice and accountability.
keywords: Guidelines for transparent, accountable student elections
The Lyngdoh Committee sought cleaner campus polls, not their abolition.
Treating adult students as unfit to decide
Suspending student polls infantilises young adults instead of trusting them with responsibility.
Students sharing in decisions that affect them
Participatory campus governance builds ownership and reduces conflict.
Time-bound commitments create graduated trust between administrations and students.
examples: Jamia's fixed timeline
Elections to be held about six weeks after 16 July 2027; disciplinary cases withdrawn
GS4
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Conflict resolution
Jamia's dispute ended only when the administration offered a fixed timeline, showing that credibility needs dates.
States reviving student polls
Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Odisha moving towards campus elections
GS2 · Education
Several states reviving student polls shows campus democracy returning to the policy agenda.
pyqs: Globalisation's impact on Indian youth, including the political sphere.
Autonomy for premier institutions: governance inside universities.
potential: "Student union elections are a nursery of democratic citizenship." Examine the case for and against their revival in Indian universities. (10 marks)

title: 'The opportunity for India is leveraging AI to reimagine how we use machines'
where: Nation, page 14 (Express Rendezvous with Kris Gopalakrishnan); TRAI draft on AI governance, Economy page 23
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: developments and their effects; Employment · GS2 › Education and skills; Regulatory bodies · GS4 › Ethics of technology
summary: Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan says AI will automate coding and freeze entry-level hiring for now, while TRAI proposes board-level accountability for AI in telecom networks.
ideas: A horizontal technology: like computing, AI affects every sector; its first effect is the 'democratisation of intelligent productivity', starting with software coding, though a human is still needed in the loop.
GS3 · Emerging technology
AI, as a horizontal technology, will reshape every sector, starting with knowledge work like coding.

The entry-level squeeze: IT revenues still grow and there are no mass layoffs, but entry-level hiring is almost zero; graduates without AI skills will struggle, and universities lag three to four years.
GS3 · Employment / GS2 · Education
AI is hitting entry-level jobs first, so curricula must catch up quickly.
India's edge is reskilling at scale: low-cost reskilling keeps margins high, and global capability centres are moving research to India.
GS3 · Industry / Human capital
Reskilling at low cost and global capability centres can turn AI disruption into an Indian advantage.
Products need risk capital: India built services without venture capital; product firms need risk capital and market access, and society needs a bigger appetite for risk.
GS3 · Startups / Investment
India's shift from services to products depends on risk capital and a culture that accepts failure.
Accountability for AI: TRAI's draft asks telecom operators to adopt board-approved AI policies and governance committees and to report AI incidents, staying liable even when AI is outsourced.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies / GS3 · Critical infrastructure
AI governance must keep humans and boards accountable, even when systems are bought from vendors.
keywords: A person checks or approves AI outputs
Keeping a human in the loop preserves accountability in AI-driven decisions.
Multinationals' in-house tech and research hubs
The growth of GCCs shows India moving up from outsourcing to research.
AI performance degrading as data change over time
TRAI flags model drift as a risk when AI runs critical networks.
Inputs designed to fool an AI system
Adversarial attacks on AI can threaten critical infrastructure.
Near-zero entry-level IT hiring is a warning of AI-led jobless growth.
data: Employed by the IT industry, out of a population of 1.4-1.5 billion
IT employs about six million people: a high-income niche, not a mass employer.
examples: TRAI's draft AI framework for telecom
Board-approved AI policies, governance committees, incident reporting
GS4
GS2 · Regulation / GS4 · Accountability
TRAI's draft shows regulators making boards answerable for AI failures.
Binance hack
About $6.3 billion stolen in some 20 minutes via a compromised engineer's laptop (Explained, page 20)
GS3 · Cyber security
The Binance hack shows how one compromised device can expose a whole financial system.
pyqs: Agentic AI: applications, risks and challenges.
Demographic dividend and falling employability: where will jobs come from?
Startups, innovation and employment, and their challenges.
AI as an input for administrative decision-making: an ethical view.
potential: "Artificial Intelligence will shrink entry-level jobs before it creates new ones." Discuss the implications for India's demographic dividend. (15 marks)
Why is board-level accountability necessary for the use of AI in critical infrastructure such as telecom? (10 marks)

title: Ashoke Sen's journey shows why science must make room for ideas yet to be tested
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: achievements of Indians; Indigenisation of technology · GS4 › Work culture and institutions
summary: String theorist Ashoke Sen is the first Indian to receive the Oskar Klein Medal; a colleague argues his career shows the value of freedom for untested theory.
ideas: Theory ahead of proof: the Klein-Gordon equation (1926) looked unconnected to nature until the Higgs boson was found in 2012; ideas can wait decades for confirmation.
GS3 · Science and technology
Basic science often pays off decades later, so it cannot be judged by immediate use.
An Indian at the frontier: Sen's 1994 work on electric-magnetic duality helped unify string theory; he is the first Indian among Oskar Klein Medal winners such as Hawking and Bethe.
GS3 · Achievements of Indians
Ashoke Sen's work shows Indian science leading at the global frontier of theory.
Institutions made it possible: Sen worked at DAE's autonomous institutes (TIFR, HRI, ICTS), where Homi Bhabha's legacy gave freedom to think and a supportive ecosystem.
GS3 · Research ecosystem / GS4 · Institutions
Autonomous institutions with freedom to think produce world-class science.
Against short-termism: string theory has faced negativity in India, partly from not understanding how frontier physics works; impatience can starve long-horizon research.
GS3 · Science policy
Science policy that demands quick results can starve long-horizon research.
keywords: Research driven by curiosity, without immediate application
Blue-sky research, like string theory, builds knowledge whose uses come later.
Freedom of research bodies from day-to-day control
Institutional autonomy at TIFR and ICTS let Indian science take long bets.
Funding must protect long-horizon research from demands for quick returns.
examples: Klein-Gordon equation and the Higgs boson
A 1926 equation confirmed by a 2012 discovery
GS3 · Science / Essay
The Klein-Gordon equation waited 86 years for the Higgs boson: patience is a scientific virtue.
Homi Bhabha's DAE ecosystem
Autonomous institutes with freedom to think
GS4
GS3 · Research / GS4 · Leadership
Bhabha's DAE shows how visionary leadership builds institutions that outlast their founders.
pyqs: Declining scientific research in Indian universities and its causes.
potential: Why is investment in basic research important for a developing country like India? Discuss the institutional conditions it needs. (10 marks)

title: To counter AI misinformation, invest in skills, literacy
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Tim Curtis, UNESCO)
syllabus: GS3 › Internal security: role of media and social networking sites; Cyber security; Science and technology: AI · GS2 › Important international institutions (UNESCO); Education (digital and media literacy); Elections · GS4 › Ethics in media and technology; Role of education in inculcating values
summary: UNESCO's South Asia head argues that laws and AI labels cannot keep pace with AI-made misinformation; India must build media and information literacy (MIL) for all, with platforms, newsrooms and creators sharing the job.
ideas: From access to judgement: generative AI makes convincing fakes cheap, so the question is no longer how to find information but how to judge what is reliable. Media and information literacy (MIL) is the answer.
GS3 · AI and misinformation
With generative AI making fakes cheap, the challenge has shifted from accessing information to judging it, which makes media and information literacy essential.
Connectivity is not capability: India has over a billion internet subscribers, but few can navigate the information space; platforms reward emotionally charged content, which deepens polarisation.
GS3 · Digital divide / social media
India's billion internet users show connectivity, not capability: only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online.
Misinformation does most harm in crises and elections, when people most need reliable information.
GS3 internal security · GS2 elections
Misinformation is most dangerous in crises and elections, as out-of-context flood videos in Nepal and a fake AI audio in Slovakia's election show.

Laws and labels are not enough: labelling AI content helps, but no law or detection tool can match the speed of synthetic content; people need skills, through trained teachers, local-language materials, and outreach beyond classrooms to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
GS3 · Way forward / GS2 education
No law or detection tool can keep pace with AI fakes; lasting defence lies in citizens' skills, taught in local languages and beyond classrooms.

'We All Play a Part': platforms must be transparent about algorithms, label synthetic media and moderate beyond English and Hindi; newsrooms must explain how they verify; creators need verification skills and ethics.
GS3 governance · GS4 media ethics
Countering misinformation is a shared duty: transparent platforms, newsrooms that explain verification, and creators trained in ethics.
MIL is an investment in democracy: children grow up in AI-shaped feeds before they can question them, so MIL builds critical thinking, social trust and collective resilience.
GS2 democracy · Essay
Media literacy is not just safe technology use; it is an investment in critical thinking, social trust and democratic resilience.
keywords: Ability to access, understand, evaluate and share information responsibly
Media and information literacy is the most durable defence against AI-made misinformation.
AI that creates realistic text, images, audio and video
Generative AI has made synthetic media cheap and convincing.
AI-made fake audio or video of real people
A deepfake audio before Slovakia's 2023 election shows the threat to elections.
Labelling AI content helps but cannot stop deception or the misuse of genuine footage.
Platforms promoting content that grabs attention, often emotional
Platforms built for attention amplify emotionally charged and divisive content.
Content moderation beyond English and Hindi
Policing harmful content in all Indian languages
In multilingual India, moderation must work beyond English and Hindi.
Real evidence dismissed as fake because fakes are common
The spread of deepfakes lets people dismiss genuine footage as fake: the liar's dividend.
A society's shared ability to resist manipulation
MIL builds collective resilience against disinformation.
data: Digital India / scale of the challenge
India has over a billion internet subscribers (TRAI).
People aged 15+ able to file a cybercrime complaint through the official portal
Only 18% of Indians aged 15 and above can file a cybercrime complaint online (NSO, 2025).
examples: UNESCO Global Media and Information Literacy Week (2026)
Theme: 'We All Play a Part: Media and Information Literacy for the People'
Global initiative / shared responsibility
UNESCO's 2026 MIL Week theme, 'We All Play a Part', stresses that countering misinformation is everyone's job.
Nepal floods, August 2026
Videos with images taken out of context circulated online
Misinformation in disasters
During Nepal's August floods, out-of-context videos distorted public understanding when reliable information mattered most.
UNESCO Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms
A framework for platform transparency and accountability
Best practice in platform governance
UNESCO's Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms offer a framework for transparency and accountability.
Slovakia's 2023 election
An AI-generated audio falsely implicated politicians two days before the vote
AI and elections
An AI-faked audio two days before Slovakia's 2023 election shows the risk to electoral integrity.
UNESCO's 'AI Answers. You Decide' module
Teaches learners how AI works and how to assess its outputs
Best practice in AI literacy
UNESCO's 'AI Answers. You Decide' module teaches students to question AI outputs.
pyqs: Directly usable: fake news threatens internal security; MIL complements the amended IT Rules.
Social media as a security challenge: AI-made misinformation is the newest form.
Misuse of social media: today the tool is generative AI, the answer includes literacy.
AI's risks include cheap, fast misinformation.
Disaster resilience includes reliable information; misinformation during Nepal's floods shows the risk.
Ethical issues of social media: platform, creator and user responsibility.
Relying on AI outputs without judgement is an ethical risk; MIL teaches people to question them.

trend.t: Social media has moved through the papers from a tool of terror (ISIS recruitment 2015, non-state actors 2016) to a security challenge (social media and encryption 2024) to fake news and its regulation (IT Rules 2026). GS4 has added the ethics of social media (2025) and of AI (2024, 2026).
trend.watch: Social media and misinformation have come in four GS3 papers and in GS4 2025, and AI in 2023, 2024 and 2026. AI-driven misinformation joins both threads and is a must-study topic.
focus: Deepfakes and AI misinformation in elections and public order
Media and information literacy as a long-term solution
Platform governance: IT Rules, labelling AI content, transparency of algorithms

potential: Generative AI has made misinformation cheaper and faster. Discuss the threats it poses to democracy and internal security in India and suggest a strategy that goes beyond regulation. (15 marks)
'Connectivity does not automatically translate into capability.' Examine the need for media and information literacy in India. (10 marks)
Discuss the role of digital platforms in countering misinformation. Should they be regulated more strictly? (10 marks)

title: How these physicists brought STEM to the doorstep of women, rural youth
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: awareness and popularisation · GS1 › Role of women · GS2 › Education; Role of NGOs
summary: Pune-based VigyanShaala International links rural youth and young women with STEM mentors and a free AI mentor on WhatsApp; over 20,000 young women in 28 states have joined its She for STEM programme.
ideas: Mentorship closes the access gap: curious students in remote areas often lack teachers who can answer them; sustained mentoring bridges that gap.
GS3 · S&T popularisation
VigyanShaala shows that sustained mentorship can bring science to students whose schools cannot answer their questions.
Technology scales guidance: a free AI mentor on WhatsApp ('Curie') lets a student in a remote college ask a career question at midnight.
GS3 · AI for good / Digital education
AI tools like VigyanShaala's WhatsApp mentor 'Curie' can scale career guidance to remote students.
Women in STEM and first-generation learners: over 70% of the 20,000 young women in She for STEM are first-generation learners.
GS1 · Women / GS2 education
Over 70% of the 20,000 young women in She for STEM are first-generation learners, proof that mentoring widens women's access to science.
Civil society complements the state: a non-profit network of 1,000 mentors fills gaps in science education and career guidance.
GS2 · Role of NGOs
Civil-society networks like VigyanShaala complement public science education with mentorship the state cannot provide alone.
keywords: Women's participation in science, technology, engineering and maths
Mentoring and role models are key to raising women in STEM.
Students whose parents did not reach higher education
Most She for STEM participants are first-generation learners.
Encouraging children's questions builds the scientific temper the Constitution asks of citizens.
Guidance from people who have walked the path
Role models make science careers imaginable for rural girls.
Using AI to widen access, not replace people
An AI mentor on WhatsApp is an example of AI for inclusion.
data: Young women who have joined She for STEM
Over 20,000 young women across 28 states have joined She for STEM; more than 70% are first-generation learners.
examples: VigyanShaala International (Pune)
1,000 STEM mentors, a free AI mentor on WhatsApp; Nikkei Asia Prize (2025), Schlumberger Foundation's Faculty for the Future Impact Prize (2026)
Best practice in science outreach
VigyanShaala, winner of the 2025 Nikkei Asia Prize, brings STEM mentors to rural youth and women.

A girl from an Indo-Nepal border district whose teachers could not answer her questions found mentors through VigyanShaala
Human story / essay
Diksha from Pithoragarh, whose questions outran her teachers, found her path through STEM mentoring.

Education as strategic investment: building scientific talent among rural youth and women.
